items.definition: Sentence pattern where an intransitive verb expresses complete action by itself without requiring any direct object or complement.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The candidate persevered.' Adverbials may modify the verb ('The candidate persevered quietly'), but the core syntactic pattern remains S-IV.

items.term: S-TV-DO Pattern (Subject + Transitive Verb + Direct Object)
items.definition: Sentence pattern where the verb transmits its action directly to a noun or pronoun that answers 'What?' or 'Whom?'.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Sir JC authored the comprehensive reviewer.' 'The comprehensive reviewer' is the direct receiver of the action 'authored'.

items.definition: Sentence pattern featuring a copular/linking verb followed by a noun that renames or equates with the subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Dr. Jose Rizal was an ophthalmologist and polymath.' 'Ophthalmologist' is a predicate noun renaming the subject 'Dr. Jose Rizal'.

items.definition: Sentence pattern featuring a linking verb followed by an adjective complement that describes or attributes a quality to the subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The licensure examination seemed arduous.' 'Arduous' is a predicate adjective describing the condition of 'examination'.

items.definition: Sentence pattern where a ditransitive verb transfers a direct object to or for the benefit of an indirect object recipient.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The mentor gave his students valuable mnemonic notes.' 'Students' = Indirect Object; 'valuable mnemonic notes' = Direct Object.

items.definition: Sentence pattern where a complex-transitive verb takes a direct object followed by a second noun that renames or re-classifies the direct object.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The PRC board appointed Sir JC chief reviewer.' 'Sir JC' is the Direct Object; 'chief reviewer' is the Objective Complement renaming him.

items.definition: Sentence pattern where the verb takes a direct object followed by an adjective complement that modifies or describes the resultant state of the direct object.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Thorough review makes the exam manageable.' 'Manageable' is an objective complement describing the direct object 'the exam'.

mnemonic.title: S-TV-DO-OC Adjective
items: OC Adjective = condition resulting from verb

items.definition: A verb category that syntactically licenses two distinct complements: an indirect object (recipient) and a direct object (theme).
items.rationalization: Common ditransitive verbs include give, lend, show, award, send, buy, and teach. Can undergo dative shift ('give X Y' -> 'give Y to X').

items.definition: A transitive verb that licenses exactly one complement, which functions as the direct object.
items.rationalization: Example: 'She read the syllabus.' 'Read' in this sentence takes only a single direct object ('the syllabus').

items.definition: A verb requiring both a direct object and an object complement (noun, adjective, or prepositional phrase) to complete its predication.
items.rationalization: Verbs like consider, elect, appoint, make, prove, and find. 'They considered the test fair.' Without 'fair', 'They considered the test' alters the meaning.

mnemonic.title: Complex Transitive
items: Cannot drop OC without altering meaning

items.definition: A verb that can be used transitively or intransitively, where the object of the transitive form becomes the subject of the intransitive form without changing meaning.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The wind opened the door' (transitive) versus 'The door opened' (intransitive). The entity undergoing change ('the door') occupies different grammatical slots.

mnemonic.title: Ergative Verb Key
items: Intransitive: Object verbs on its own

items.definition: A non-action verb that couples the grammatical subject with a subject complement asserting an identity, condition, or sensory attribute.
items.rationalization: Includes forms of 'be' (am, is, are, was, were) and sensory verbs (seem, appear, look, smell, taste, feel, become, remain).

items.definition: Syntactic transformation converting an S-TV-IO-DO structure into an S-TV-DO-PrepO structure (or vice versa).
items.rationalization: Example: 'The teacher handed Maria the certificate' (S-TV-IO-DO) becomes 'The teacher handed the certificate to Maria' (S-TV-DO-PrepO).

mnemonic.title: Dative Shift
mnemonic.phrase: Shift IO to Prepositional Phrase with 'To/For'

items.definition: A Direct Object receives the action of a transitive verb and is not identical to the subject; a Predicate Noun follows a linking verb and equates with the subject.
items.rationalization: In 'John made a chair', 'chair' is a Direct Object (John != chair). In 'John became a chairman', 'chairman' is a Predicate Noun (John == chairman).

mnemonic.title: DO vs PN Contrast
mnemonic.phrase: DO is Acted Upon; PN Equates with Subject

items.definition: An Indirect Object receives the Direct Object (IO != DO); an Objective Complement renames or describes the Direct Object (DO == OC).
items.rationalization: In 'We gave John a medal', John != medal (IO-DO). In 'We crowned John champion', John == champion (DO-OC).

mnemonic.title: OC vs IO Test
mnemonic.phrase: IO: Two Different Entities; OC: Same Entity (DO=OC)
items: IO: X gives Y to Z
OC: X declares Y to be Z

items.definition: A dummy or placeholder syntactic element occupying the subject position in an existential clause while the true logical subject follows the verb.
items.rationalization: Example: 'There are forty questions in this section.' The true subject is 'forty questions' (plural), which governs the plural verb 'are'.

mnemonic.title: Expletive There
mnemonic.phrase: There = Dummy Seat-Holder; Real Subject Follows

items.definition: A non-referential pronoun used as a syntactic subject for ambient weather conditions, time, distance, or extraposed clauses.
items.rationalization: Example: 'It is important that teachers master syntax.' 'It' carries no semantic antecedent; the extraposed that-clause is the logical proposition.

items.definition: A complex sentence construction beginning with 'It + be + focused constituent + that/who clause' designed to emphasize a specific syntactic element.
items.rationalization: From 'Claro M. Recto authored the bill', the It-cleft produces: 'It was Claro M. Recto who authored the bill.' Focus is highlighted on Recto.

mnemonic.title: It-Cleft Focus
mnemonic.phrase: Cleave to Highlight Focus: It is X that...

items.definition: A cleft sentence construction beginning with a free relative clause introduced by 'what' followed by a linking verb and the focal phrase.
items.rationalization: Example: 'What future teachers need is relentless discipline.' Highlights the nominal complement 'relentless discipline'.

items.definition: A structural transformation wherein the direct object of an active transitive verb is promoted to grammatical subject, and the original agent is relegated to an optional 'by' prepositional phrase.
items.rationalization: Active: 'The proctor monitored the room.' -> Passive: 'The room was monitored by the proctor.' Aux 'be' + past participle is obligatory.

mnemonic.title: Passive Voice Formula
mnemonic.phrase: Promote Object to Subject + BE + Past Participle

items.definition: A full sentence inversion where a directional or prepositional phrase of location precedes an intransitive verb, followed by the subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Into the examination room marched the confident test-takers.' Verb 'marched' agrees with post-verbal subject 'test-takers'.

items.definition: A complement is an obligatory constituent required by a head verb to complete grammatical sense; an adjunct is an optional modifier that can be omitted freely.
items.rationalization: In 'She put the book on the desk', 'on the desk' is an obligatory locative complement. In 'She read the book on the desk', 'on the desk' is an optional adjunct.

mnemonic.title: Complement vs Adjunct
mnemonic.phrase: Complement is Compulsory; Adjunct is Add-on

items.definition: Syntactic constraint where verbs describing permanent states, cognition, or possession generally disallow progressive (-ing) aspect.
items.rationalization: Standard English: 'I know the answer' (NOT 'I am knowing the answer'). Stative verbs include believe, understand, resemble, own, and contain.

items.definition: An -ing verbal noun filling the primary nominal subject slot of a sentence governing a singular verb.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Mastering sentence patterns guarantees high marks on the English majorship exam.' 'Mastering sentence patterns' is the singular gerund phrase subject.

items.definition: An -ing verbal nominal occurring after a linking verb that identifies or specifies the nature of the grammatical subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Her greatest passion is teaching literature.' 'Teaching literature' is a gerund phrase serving as the predicate noun/subject complement.

items.definition: A to-infinitive phrase functioning as the direct receiver of an action governed by verbs of intention, desire, or planning.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The examinees planned to achieve top honors.' 'To achieve top honors' answers 'What did they plan?' (Direct Object).

items.definition: A Gerund functions strictly as a noun; a Present Participle functions as an adjective or forms part of a continuous verb tense.
items.rationalization: In 'Sleeping is essential' -> Gerund (Subject). In 'The sleeping student missed the tip' -> Participle (Adjective modifying student).

items.definition: A syntactic error where an introductory participial phrase lacks a logical subject in the immediately following independent clause.
items.rationalization: Error: 'Walking into the classroom, the exam was already distributed.' (The exam was not walking). Correction: 'Walking into the classroom, the teacher noticed the exams.'

mnemonic.title: Dangling Modifier Fix
mnemonic.phrase: Who Did the -ing? Place Them Right After the Comma!

items.definition: A syntactic flaw where a modifier is separated too far from the word it is intended to describe, causing unintentional ambiguity.
items.rationalization: Error: 'Sir JC reviewed the item with the student that was difficult.' (Was the student difficult?). Correction: 'Sir JC reviewed the difficult item with the student.'

mnemonic.title: Misplaced Modifier
mnemonic.phrase: Keep Modifiers Next to What They Modify

items.definition: A dependent clause introduced by that, whether, or a wh-word that fulfills the grammatical function of a sentence subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'That Filipino teachers are globally competent is universally recognized.' The entire clause 'That Filipino teachers are globally competent' is the subject.

mnemonic.title: Noun Clause Subject
mnemonic.phrase: Whole Clause Acts as One Noun

items.definition: Restrictive clauses provide essential identification without commas ('that/who'); non-restrictive clauses supply non-essential parenthetical detail enclosed by commas ('which/who').
items.rationalization: Restrictive: 'Teachers who inspire change shape society.' Non-restrictive: 'Sir JC, who created the reviewer, teaches future educators.'

items.definition: Agreement principle applied when subjects are joined by 'or', 'nor', 'either...or', or 'neither...nor', requiring the verb to agree with the subject closest to it.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers were present.' (Plural 'teachers' is nearest to 'were'). 'Neither the teachers nor the principal was present.'

items.definition: Collective nouns take a singular verb when the group acts as a unified whole, and a plural verb when individual members act separately.
items.rationalization: Unit: 'The PRC board has issued the schedule.' Individuals: 'The faculty have debated their varying perspectives.'

mnemonic.title: Collective Noun Test
mnemonic.phrase: One Unit = Singular; Divided Members = Plural

items.definition: Sentence pattern initiated by negative or restrictive adverbs (rarely, seldom, scarcely, never, not only) requiring subject-auxiliary inversion.
items.rationalization: Example: 'Rarely do prospective examinees encounter such clear explanations.' Aux 'do' precedes subject 'examinees'.

mnemonic.title: Negative Inversion
mnemonic.phrase: Negative Word First -> Aux Before Subject

items.definition: Rule requiring that elements connected by paired conjunctions (not only...but also, both...and, either...or) match in identical syntactic form.
items.rationalization: Faulty: 'He not only studied phonology, but also syntax.' Better: 'He studied not only phonology but also syntax.' (Both connect direct object nouns).

items.definition: Verbal mood used in that-clauses after verbs of demand, recommendation, or necessity, utilizing the bare base form of the verb regardless of subject.
items.rationalization: Example: 'The dean recommended that every candidate attend the session.' (Not 'attends'). Verbs include insist, recommend, demand, require.

items.definition: A linguistic phenomenon where a single surface sentence can be parsed with two or more distinct underlying hierarchical syntactic tree structures.
items.rationalization: Classic LET example: 'The teacher watched the student with binoculars.' (Who had the binoculars: the teacher or the student?).

items.definition: Chomskyan Generative Grammar concept where Deep Structure represents abstract syntactic/semantic meaning and Surface Structure represents phonetic/linear sentence output.
items.rationalization: 'The boy graded the quiz' and 'The quiz was graded by the boy' share identical Deep Structure semantic roles despite divergent Surface Structures.

mnemonic.title: Deep vs Surface Structure
mnemonic.phrase: Deep = Core Meaning; Surface = Spoken Order

items.definition: Linguistic diagnostic procedures (pro-form substitution, topicalization, clefting, fragment test) used to determine whether a sequence of words behaves as a single syntactic unit.
items.rationalization: If a group of words can be replaced by a single pronoun ('The tall teacher in the room' -> 'She') or moved to sentence front, it is a constituent.

items.definition: A verb that can link directly with another verb form (infinitive or gerund) in a chain without intervening coordinating conjunctions.
items.rationalization: Example: 'She seems to want to try answering the question.' 'Seems', 'want', 'try' form a catenative chain.

mnemonic.title: Catenative Chain
items: Verbs that link to subordinate verbs

items.definition: Principle in Government and Binding Theory stating that each argument is assigned exactly one thematic role (Agent, Theme, Goal, Experiencer) and each thematic role is assigned to exactly one argument.
items.rationalization: Prevents syntactic anomalies by ensuring predicate argument structures match semantic roles in sentence generation.
